content: The recommendation will be disseminated through various channels, including WHO regional and country offices, ministries of health, professional organizations, WHO collaborating centers, other United Nations agencies, and nongovernmental organizations. It will also be published on the WHO Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH) Department website and included in the WHO Human Reproduction Programme News bulletin, which reaches over 8,000 subscribers worldwide, including clinicians, health program managers, policymakers, and service users. Updated recommendations are routinely shared during meetings or scientific conferences attended by WHO maternal and perinatal health staff. The executive summary and recommendations from this publication will be translated into the six official United Nations languages and disseminated through WHO regional offices. National and subnational subgroups may be established to adapt and implement the recommendation based on existing strategies. This process may involve developing or revising national guidelines or protocols. The successful introduction of evidence-based policies depends on well-planned, participatory, and consensus-driven processes of adaptation and implementation. These processes may include revising existing national or local guidelines and protocols, often supported by ministries of health, United Nations agencies, local professional societies, and other relevant leadership groups. An enabling environment should be created to facilitate the use of this recommendation, including changes in healthcare practitioners' behavior to adopt evidence-based practices. The recommendation should be adapted into documents and tools, such as clinical care pathways, tailored to different locations and contexts to meet the specific needs of each country and health service. Any modifications to the recommendations should be explicitly and transparently justified. In humanitarian emergencies, adaptation of the recommendation should consider integration and alignment with other response strategies, as well as the unique needs, values, and preferences of women in such settings. Context-specific tools and toolkits may be required in addition to standard tools to support implementation in humanitarian emergencies. To assess the feasibility of implementing universal screening, several factors should be considered: (i) the incidence of Group B Streptococcus (GBS) colonization, (ii) the availability of trained health workers to counsel pregnant women and ensure swab collection during antenatal care, (iii) access to and capacity of laboratories to process bacteriological cultures, and (iv) continuity of care to ensure that all women who screen positive during pregnancy receive intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP). Healthcare providers' knowledge and skills should be strengthened regarding counseling, screening strategies, antibiotic use, and the provision of culturally sensitive, woman-centered care around GBS screening, particularly as screening may cause maternal anxiety. Settings may implement self-swabbing or swabbing by healthcare workers, as evidence suggests that women's preferences for self-swabbing versus professional swabbing vary, and self-swabbing remains accurate. Lower vaginal and rectal swabbing should be performed without a speculum. Clear information and decision-support about the screening procedure should be provided to women, including instructions for self-swabbing if needed. Health facilities implementing universal screening should ensure they have adequately trained staff, clear protocols, and the necessary equipment and supplies to store and process laboratory samples. A well-defined process is needed to ensure continuity between antenatal care, receipt of test results, and eligibility for IAP at admission for birth. Streamlined communication and coordination are required throughout the screening process. WHO recommendations for a positive pregnancy experience suggest an antenatal contact at 36 weeks, during which GBS testing could occur. Health facilities providing IAP should ensure they have adequately trained staff, clear protocols, and the necessary equipment and supplies to safely administer intravenous drugs and manage complications if they arise. Antibiotic regimens should be determined according to local protocols. Settings may consider: (i) 2 g of ampicillin IV followed by 1 g every 4 hours until birth; (ii) 500 mg of ampicillin IV every 6 hours until birth; or (iii) 5 million units of penicillin G IV every 6 hours during labor, with 1 million units orally every 8 hours if labor lasts more than 18 hours. Maternal screening strategies do not prevent all cases of early-onset GBS disease and do not reduce the risk of late-onset GBS disease. Prompt recognition and early initiation of appropriate antimicrobial therapy are necessary to minimize morbidity and mortality among cases that continue to occur. WHO has existing recommendations for managing severe bacterial infections in young infants (0–59 days). Mechanisms should be in place at health facilities to ensure that necessary drugs are securely stored and available when needed. A hospital committee is essential to monitor antimicrobial usage, including the quantity and patterns of use. The committee should report results to prescribers and regularly update the hospital antimicrobial formularies. Where penicillin and its derivatives are contraindicated, alternative antibiotics should be made available. Penicillin and ampicillin must be transported and stored according to supplier specifications. As these antibiotics are heat-sensitive and may require refrigeration, proper storage may not be feasible in settings with inconsistent electricity supply. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) identified critical knowledge gaps that need to be addressed through primary research, which may impact this recommendation. Key questions include: (i) In lowand middle-income countries, is universal or risk-based screening more effective, acceptable, feasible, and cost-effective? (ii) Is rapid intrapartum testing for GBS effective compared to antepartum testing for IAP in preventing early-onset GBS disease in newborns? (iii) What are the shortand long-term impacts of IAP on newborn and child health, including effects on the intestinal microbiota, developmental outcomes, and chronic disease? Several barriers may hinder the effective implementation and scale-up of this recommendation. These barriers may relate to the behaviors of women, parents, caregivers, families, or health workers, as well as the organization of care or health service delivery. Potential barriers include: (i) lack of understanding of GBS and the purpose of GBS screening among health workers, birthing women, families, and communities; (ii) lack of opportunities for continuing education and professional development for health workers; (iii) lack of human resources with the necessary training and skills in patient communication, consent, infection control, rectovaginal swab techniques, specimen handling, and administration of intravenous IAP; (iv) lack of infrastructure to support interventions, such as physical space for individual care and counseling, access to laboratory services for culture-based testing, and reliable electricity for refrigeration; (v) concerns from skilled care personnel and system managers regarding the safety and potential consequences of intravenous IAP, including antimicrobial resistance; (vi) lack of reliable supply systems and sustained availability and equitable access to antibiotics for obstetric use listed in the WHO model list of essential medicines; and (vii) lack of systems to monitor antibiotic use and antimicrobial resistance. The implementation and impact of this recommendation will be monitored at health service, country, and regional levels as part of broader efforts to improve the quality of maternal and newborn care. The WHO document Standards for improving quality of maternal and newborn care in health facilities provides a list of prioritized input, output, and outcome measures that can be used to define quality of care criteria and indicators aligned with locally agreed targets. Data on countryand regional-level implementation of the recommendation can be collected and evaluated in the short to medium term to assess its impact on national policies. Information on recommended indicators can also be obtained at the local level through interrupted time series or clinical audits. Suggested indicators include: (i) the proportion of women undergoing screening for the risk of early-onset GBS disease in newborns where IAP was administered for eligible women, and (ii) the incidence of early-onset GBS disease in newborns. The Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) convenes annually to review WHO’s portfolio of maternal and perinatal health recommendations and prioritize new and existing questions for recommendation development and updating. This recommendation will be reviewed alongside others for prioritization by the Executive GSG. If new evidence that could impact the current evidence base is identified, the recommendation may be updated. If no new reports or information are identified, the recommendation may be revalidated. The GDG acknowledged the anticipated publication of the GBS3 trial in 2026, which will provide new evidence on universal screening (including rapid intrapartum testing) compared to risk-based screening. The GDG also noted the prioritized development of GBS vaccines suitable for maternal immunization during pregnancy and for use in lowand middle-income countries by WHO. Following publication and dissemination of the updated recommendation, any concerns about its validity should be promptly communicated to guideline implementers. WHO welcomes suggestions regarding additional questions for inclusion in any updated recommendation.
